title: Daytona Pricing 2026: Sandbox Costs and Free Credits
summary: Idle sandboxes cost more in Daytona's pricing model than active compute, making this distinction essential for accurate infrastructure budgeting.
body_markdown:
## What Daytona costs at realistic usage levels


**An always-on 2 vCPU / 4 GiB sandbox costs about $121 a month, so idle time is the largest cost you control.** Split out, that is $73.584 for vCPU, $47.304 for memory and $0 for disk, according to[Boxyard](https://boxyard.dev/providers/daytona/pricing) .


On a log scale,[Agent37](https://www.agent37.com/blog/daytona-pricing) 's chart compares developer testing, **100,000 one-minute runs at $276.00** , and an always-on month at roughly $120.89 to $122.07.


For a solo prototype, a handful of short sessions a week costs cents, so the free credits cover it. One sandbox left running all month costs the full $120.888, which is why the idle interval matters more than anything you build.


For a small team with bursty agent runs, 100,000 one-minute runs add up to about 1,667 sandbox-hours. That's more than double the 730 hours in a month, which is possible because the runs overlap across parallel sandboxes.


At $0.1656 an hour for this size, that's the $276.00 for the batch.


Here, auto-stop doesn't save you, since the sandboxes were never idle. Per-run time is the lever, so trim startup and setup work inside each run.


### Always-on sandboxes per user


At about $121 each, one persistent sandbox per user puts 50 users at roughly $6,044 a month. Auto-stop pays off most here, because users rarely work around the clock. Every hour a stopped sandbox isn't billed comes straight off that total.


Three things would overturn the idle-time conclusion. The first is run volume high enough that active seconds outweigh idle ones, as in the 100,000-run case.


The second is larger sandboxes, which scale the vCPU and memory lines. The third is disk usage beyond whatever allowance makes the $0 line true, which would put a third charge on the bill.
